cases.case_name: In re Interest of B.B.
cases.holding: The court held that the reporter-immunity provision of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-716 protects a person who makes a mandated child abuse or neglect report from civil or criminal liability but does not bar the juvenile court from acquiring jurisdiction over the reporting parent and her children under § 43-247(3)(a).
cases.quote: they are designed to compel notification of child abuse or neglect to proper authorities in order to place such children and their parents under the supervision of the juvenile court

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Nebraska appellate construction of the mandatory-reporting scheme in Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 28-710 to 28-727, explaining what the duty to report is for and how far the reporter's statutory immunity reaches.
relevance.INP-02: The § 28-716 immunity the court construes runs to 'any person participating in ... the making of a report,' not only to listed professionals, which is the legal footing for voluntary third-party reports.
relevance.INP-05: The reporting party here was the children's own mother seeking help with a child she could not keep safely at home, and the court held her self-report did not immunize her from juvenile-court jurisdiction.
relevance.INP-06: The court reads § 28-716 immunity as attaching to the act of reporting itself, which is the protection on which confidential and hotline reports rest, subject to the exception for maliciously false statements.
relevance.INP-08: Section 28-711, which the court parses, names school employees and social workers among the professionals whose observations trigger the reporting duty.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of R.G.
cases.holding: The court held that an ex parte temporary detention order is not itself a final, appealable order, that henceforth the information supporting such an order must be presented by affidavit of a person with knowledge of the relevant facts, and that the mother's due process rights were satisfied because she received a meaningful opportunity to be heard at the subsequent detention hearing.
cases.quote: Due process principles therefore require that the mother have been given a meaningful opportunity to be heard on the issue of whether a detention order should have been issued.

relevance.INP-12: This is the foundational Nebraska decision on what process is constitutionally owed a parent when the State takes a child into protective custody before any adjudication.
relevance.DEC-04: It fixes the affidavit requirement and the post-removal hearing right that govern every emergency removal decision made ahead of a court order.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal carried out without a supporting affidavit and without a prompt, meaningful hearing is the paradigm of the procedural defect this decision identifies.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Borius H.
cases.holding: The court reaffirmed that every motion for an ex parte temporary detention order must be supported by an affidavit of a person with knowledge, held that the State must prove the requirements of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-254 by a preponderance of the evidence at the detention hearing, and ordered dismissal because the State adduced no evidence at that hearing.
cases.quote: we once again state that all motions for ex parte temporary detention orders must be accompanied by an affidavit of one who has knowledge of relevant facts warranting temporary detention

relevance.INP-03: The removal here began with a county attorney's motion following a law-enforcement and agency referral, and the court specifies the evidentiary showing that referral must be reduced to.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from report to State custody cannot rest on the caseworker's say-so; the court requires a sworn factual predicate.
relevance.INP-12: It states the affidavit prerequisite for taking emergency protective custody by ex parte order.
relevance.DEC-04: It supplies the burden of proof — preponderance — that the State carries at the hearing that must follow an emergency removal decision.
relevance.DEC-05: The decision governs the county attorney's motion for temporary custody filed alongside the juvenile petition.
relevance.OUT-05: Because the State offered no evidence at the detention hearing, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded with orders to dismiss, illustrating dismissal for failure of proof.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a direct appellate reversal of a custody order the agency and county attorney obtained on an inadequate record.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Carmelo G.
cases.holding: The court held that a delay of more than eight months between entry of an ex parte temporary custody order and the protective custody order was unreasonable and violated the mother's procedural due process rights.
cases.quote: due process rights include the right to be free from an unreasonable delay in providing a parent a meaningful hearing after the entry of an ex parte temporary custody order

relevance.INP-02: The case opened on reports of parental drug use and domestic violence and shows how such reports are converted into an ex parte custody order.
relevance.INP-03: The record describes the coordinated law-enforcement and DHHS response that produced the affidavit for removal.
relevance.INP-06: The intake allegations that triggered removal were third-party reports of drug use and domestic violence, screened in and acted on the same day.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion describes safety plans put in place when a child is at risk of removal absent services, and the escalation from safety plan to protective custody.
relevance.INP-12: It is the leading recent Nebraska statement of the timeliness component of due process once protective custody is taken.
relevance.DEC-02: The affidavit and safety-assessment practices described frame what an accepted investigation looks like in Nebraska before removal.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that the emergency removal decision is only lawful if followed by a meaningful hearing without unreasonable delay.
relevance.DEC-06: The court describes safety plans and in-home services used to avert removal, the practical analogue to alternative response.
relevance.ACT-01: Safety plans with voluntary services are described as the tool used when services can keep the child at home.
relevance.ACT-05: The protective custody order and attendant conditions are the juvenile-court mechanism Nebraska uses in place of a freestanding protective order.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed for a procedural due process violation arising from the agency's and court's delay.
relevance.FAIL-02: An extended, unexcused delay in providing the post-removal hearing renders the continued deprivation of custody constitutionally infirm.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Xandria P.
cases.holding: The court held that the child's recorded child-advocacy-center forensic interview was properly admitted under the rule 803(3) medical diagnosis or treatment exception and that the State proved the allegations of the § 43-247(3)(a) petition by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: we conclude that the State sustained the adjudication petition by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-01: The investigation began from a report by the child's teacher, the classic mandated-reporter pathway.
relevance.INP-06: The child's disclosure reached the agency through school and hotline channels before the forensic interview was conducted.
relevance.INP-07: The court holds the forensic interview admissible because the child was told the center was part of a hospital and that a doctor or nurse would be available, bringing the statements within the medical diagnosis exception.
relevance.INP-08: A school disclosure started the case, and the teacher's out-of-court statements were themselves at issue on appeal.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion traces the escalation from school report through forensic interview and safety and risk assessments to a filed petition.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the Nebraska Supreme Court's most recent guidance on how child forensic interviews conducted during an accepted investigation may be used as evidence.
relevance.DEC-03: The evidentiary rulings define what agency investigative product — forensic interviews, safety and risk assessments — can support a founded finding.
relevance.DEC-05: It states the burden the State carries on the petition it files to open a dependency case.
relevance.ACT-06: The child-advocacy-center protocol described includes access to a physician or nurse immediately after the interview.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jeremy U.
cases.holding: The court held that 'lacks proper parental care' in § 43-247(3)(a) refers to the type and nature of the care a child is receiving rather than to who provides it, so the two children living safely with grandparents could not be adjudicated on that ground, while the child living with the mother should have been adjudicated.
cases.quote: We conclude that "parental" as used in the phrase "lacks proper parental care" describes the type and nature of care rather than the relationship of the person providing it.

relevance.DEC-01: It marks the line between facts that warrant State intervention and facts that do not, which is the substance of a screen-out or unfounded determination.
relevance.DEC-05: The court tells the State it may petition again only if it acquires evidence that the children actually lack proper care, constraining petition practice.
relevance.OUT-05: The adjudications of two of the three children were reversed for insufficient evidence, the appellate form of case dismissal.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a Nebraska Supreme Court reversal of an adjudication the agency obtained on legally insufficient grounds.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of DeWayne G., Jr.
cases.holding: The court held that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-283.01 gives a parent no right to demand a separate pre-termination hearing on whether reasonable efforts to preserve and reunify the family were made, and reinstated the termination of parental rights.
cases.quote: the plain language of § 43-283.01 contains no such directive granting a parent or any other party the right to bring a motion requesting a "separate hearing"

relevance.DEC-01: The reasonable-efforts framework of § 43-283.01 is the statutory backdrop against which front-end decisions to intervene or not are measured.
relevance.DEC-05: The opinion sets out the reasonable-efforts findings the juvenile court must make in the course of the dependency case the State opens.
relevance.DEC-06: Section 43-283.01(2), quoted by the court, requires efforts to preserve families before foster placement — the statutory basis for non-court service responses.
relevance.ACT-01: The statute the court construes directs that reasonable efforts be made to prevent the need for removal, which is the mandate behind voluntary service plans.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines how reasonable efforts to reunify are litigated within the ordinary course of the case rather than in a standalone proceeding.
relevance.OUT-01: The court notes that priority must be given to preserving and reunifying the family even when adoption or guardianship efforts proceed concurrently.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is Nebraska's construction of the state-law codification of the federal Title IV-E reasonable-efforts condition on funding.
relevance.PMC-01: The reasonable-efforts judicial determinations at issue are the same determinations federal CFSR and IV-E reviews audit.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Leyton C. & Landyn C.
cases.holding: The court held that the State proved by clear and convincing evidence both a statutory ground under § 43-292 and that termination was in the children's best interests, and reversed the Court of Appeals' contrary decision.
cases.quote: The State proved by clear and convincing evidence that Madison neglected to provide necessary parental care and protection for her children.

relevance.DEC-03: The neglect finding the court sustains shows what evidence of failure to provide necessary parental care and protection looks like in Nebraska.
relevance.OUT-01: The mother's failure over the case's life to correct the conditions that caused removal is what foreclosed reunification.
relevance.OUT-02: It states and applies the two-part clear-and-convincing test — statutory ground plus best interests — that governs every Nebraska termination.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jessalina M.
cases.holding: The court held that the § 43-292(7) statutory ground was properly found, that changed conditions between petition and hearing bear on fitness and best interests rather than on the statutory ground, and affirmed the termination of parental rights.
cases.quote: if conditions have changed since the time the petition was filed to the time of the hearing, the court is advised to factor those changes into its determination of fitness

relevance.OUT-02: It fixes the timing rule for the § 43-292(7) ground and confirms that unfitness and best interests are reviewed separately from the mechanical statutory basis.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Mainor T.
cases.holding: The court held that plain error permeated the proceedings because the mother had a statutory right to counsel under § 43-279.01 but was unrepresented and had not waived counsel at adjudication, and that she was denied due process; the abandonment finding and the termination of her parental rights were reversed.
cases.quote: Our de novo review of the record demonstrates that during these proceedings, Mercedes was denied due process.

relevance.DEC-05: The due process defects the court identifies begin at the filing and adjudication stage, not at termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the leading Nebraska authority that an unrepresented, unwarned parent cannot have her rights terminated consistent with due process.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed the entire chain of orders for fundamental unfairness, including the abandonment finding and the termination.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Walter W.
cases.holding: The court held that the ICWA and Nebraska ICWA 'active efforts' element must be proved by clear and convincing evidence rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the Department met that burden, affirming the termination.
cases.quote: we decline to interpret § 1912(d) — and its Nebraska counterpart, § 43-1505(4) — as requiring the State to prove active efforts beyond a reasonable doubt

relevance.INP-11: This is Nebraska's controlling decision on the burden the State bears under ICWA and the Nebraska ICWA once a case involves an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines the heightened 'active efforts' remedial and rehabilitative service obligation that replaces ordinary reasonable efforts in ICWA cases.
relevance.OUT-02: The opinion sets out the layered ICWA proof structure, including the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt qualified-expert-witness finding required before termination.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to make and prove active efforts is the ICWA compliance failure most often raised on appeal in Nebraska.
relevance.FAIL-05: ICWA's requirements exist to prevent the disproportionate break-up of Indian families, and this case states how Nebraska enforces them.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of Eliza W.
cases.holding: The court held that a guardianship proceeding brought by a private individual over an Indian child is a 'foster care placement' within ICWA and the Nebraska ICWA, so the Act's protections — including active efforts, qualified expert witness testimony, and counsel for an indigent parent — apply.
cases.quote: we are not persuaded by Susan's arguments that the guardianship proceeding she initiated does not qualify as a "foster care placement" under ICWA and NICWA

relevance.INP-11: It is the Nebraska Supreme Court's definitive statement of when ICWA and the Nebraska ICWA attach, reaching private proceedings and not only State-initiated ones.
relevance.ACT-04: A guardianship with a non-parent caregiver is treated as a foster care placement, so the Act's placement preferences and expert-witness rules govern it.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency through guardianship of an Indian child cannot be ordered without ICWA compliance.
relevance.FAIL-05: The decision closes a route by which ICWA's anti-discrimination protections could be bypassed through a privately filed guardianship.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Mercedes L.
cases.holding: The court held the November orders were final and appealable, affirmed on the ICWA issues raised by the incarcerated mother, but held that the December orders appointing guardians for the children were void for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and vacated them.
cases.quote: we affirm, but we hold that the court's orders of December 12, 2017, appointing a guardian for each of the children are void for lack of subject matter jurisdiction

relevance.INP-11: The opinion applies ICWA and the Nebraska ICWA to active efforts, qualified expert witness testimony, and deviation from the placement preferences in a Nebraska juvenile case.
relevance.ACT-04: It addresses the showing of good cause required before the court departs from ICWA's relative and tribal placement preferences.
relevance.OUT-03: It marks the jurisdictional limit on a juvenile court's power to appoint guardians for an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Deviation from ICWA placement preferences must be justified on the record, which is the safeguard against placement bias.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jackson E.
cases.holding: The court held that foster parents, including one who was also the child's maternal grandmother, lack standing to appeal a juvenile court order changing the child's placement, and dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
cases.quote: As foster parents, Erin and Paul do not have standing to appeal the change in Jackson's placement.

relevance.ACT-03: It fixes who may and may not contest a foster placement decision on appeal in Nebraska.
relevance.ACT-04: The grandmother-caregiver's kinship status did not give her standing, an important limit on kinship caregivers' procedural rights.
relevance.FAIL-01: It defines the narrow class of parties who can obtain appellate review of an agency placement change.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jordon B.
cases.holding: The court held that foster parents have a statutory right to participate in review hearings but no right to intervene as parties or to appeal a placement order, and that the adult adoptive relative was not a 'sibling' entitled to intervene.
cases.quote: We conclude that as foster parents, the Todds did not have the right to intervene as parties and did not have the right to appeal the juvenile court's placement order.

relevance.ACT-03: It is the most recent Nebraska Supreme Court statement of foster parents' procedural role in placement decisions.
relevance.ACT-04: The court construes 'sibling' under the Foster Care Review Act in deciding who may press a joint-sibling placement claim.
relevance.OUT-03: It limits who may intervene to contest permanency and placement outcomes short of the parties to the juvenile case.
relevance.PMC-03: The court describes the statutory review-hearing participation right that is the state-level analogue to independent citizen review of placements.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Mekhi S.
cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court retains jurisdiction over a child after placing the child in a guardianship, so it had authority to entertain the guardian ad litem's motion to terminate the disrupted guardianship and return the children to DHHS custody.
cases.quote: the parents' rights have not been terminated, and Nebraska jurisprudence dictates that a juvenile court retains jurisdiction over a juvenile after it places the child in a guardianship

relevance.INP-04: The juvenile court's retained jurisdiction is what permits a court-initiated return of a child to agency custody after a permanency order.
relevance.INP-05: The proceeding was reopened on the guardian ad litem's own motion alleging the guardianship had disrupted.
relevance.OUT-01: Continued juvenile court jurisdiction is the mechanism through which a child whose permanency plan fails can be returned to agency care and services.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling Nebraska authority on a juvenile court's power over a guardianship permanency placement after it is ordered.
relevance.OUT-04: Retained jurisdiction after a permanency order is the structural predicate for continued agency responsibility for an older youth.

cases.case_name: Calkins ex rel. Antonio S. v. Nebraska Department of Health & Human Services
cases.holding: The court held that duly appointed guardians take both care and custody of the children and that the juvenile court did not err in relieving DHHS of custody, case management and supervision, even though that ended the children's prospective eligibility for the State's former ward program.
cases.quote: did not err in ordering that Marlin and Sharon, as duly appointed guardians, shall have the care and custody of Priscilla and Antonio

relevance.INP-05: The guardian ad litem brought the request to preserve the children's benefit eligibility, showing how a child's advocate can initiate a change in the agency's role.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines the legal consequence of a kinship guardianship: care and custody transfer together and the agency's supervisory role ends.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the Nebraska Supreme Court's treatment of the former ward program — the State's transitional supports for youth leaving care — and of the trade-off between guardianship permanency and continued eligibility.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Kate S.
cases.holding: The court held that petitioners seeking to dispense with a parent's adoption consent on abandonment grounds must prove willful abandonment by clear and convincing evidence, and affirmed the county court's finding that the father had not abandoned the child.
cases.quote: The conduct constituting abandonment must appear by clear and convincing evidence to be willful, intentional, or voluntary, without just cause or excuse.

relevance.OUT-02: It states Nebraska's standard for proceeding to adoption without a parent's consent, the stepparent-adoption analogue to termination.
relevance.OUT-03: Adoption is one of the permanency outcomes, and this case sets the consent and abandonment prerequisites for it.
relevance.OUT-05: The adoption petition was denied for failure of proof, and that denial was affirmed.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Maximus B.
cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court order at issue was not a final order affecting a substantial right of the State and dismissed the State's appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction.
cases.quote: We conclude that the March 27, 2018, order from which this case arises is not a final order appealable by the State, and we therefore dismiss this appeal.

relevance.INP-04: The court explains that the State's appealable interest in a juvenile proceeding derives from its parens patriae duty to protect resident children.
relevance.OUT-04: Appealability in juvenile proceedings turns on the substantial-right analysis this case applies, which governs challenges to continuing-jurisdiction orders.
relevance.OUT-05: Dismissal for want of a final order is one of the principal ways juvenile appeals end without a merits ruling.
relevance.FAIL-01: It states the finality rule that determines when an agency or State decision in a juvenile case can be reviewed at all.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Veskrna v. Steel
cases.holding: The court held that the requested judicial branch education records were public records under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 84-712.01 with no applicable statutory exception, and affirmed the mandamus judgment compelling their disclosure with one internal email redacted, together with costs and attorney fees.
cases.quote: we affirm the judgment of the district court granting Veskrna access to the records found in exhibit 4, with the specified email redacted

relevance.INP-09: Public records litigation is the principal citizen tool for surfacing the systemic data that triggers oversight inquiries.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is Nebraska's leading modern decision on an agency's refusal to disclose records and the mandamus remedy under § 84-712.03.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and financial records held by state bodies are public records unless an express statutory exception applies.
relevance.PMC-03: The decision rejects reliance on an unwritten internal confidentiality policy, which is the same defense that defeats transparency for review-panel records.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review materials held by state entities are subject to the same public-records analysis absent an express exemption.
relevance.PMC-05: It establishes the burden, procedure and fee-shifting for a Nebraska public records demand — the state-law counterpart to FOIA.

cases.case_name: Joshua M. v. State
cases.holding: The court held that the siblings' negligence claims against DHHS arising from years of sexual and physical abuse by their foster father fall within the State Tort Claims Act's exemption for claims arising out of assault or battery, so sovereign immunity was not waived and the district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction.
cases.quote: because we conclude the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the siblings' claims against DHHS, we do not reach the merits of any assigned error

relevance.INP-09: The opinion recounts conflicting evidence about whether abuse in the foster home was reported to DHHS and how the agency responded, the factual core of any systemic review.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling Nebraska decision on the State's tort exposure when a child in its care suffers serious injury at a caregiver's hands.
relevance.FAIL-04: Children abused while under agency supervision have no damages remedy against DHHS in Nebraska where the harm arises out of assault or battery.
relevance.FAIL-06: Because the claim is dismissed on jurisdictional grounds, the agency's conduct is never adjudicated on the record.
relevance.PMC-01: Outcomes like this one are precisely the safety failures federal CFSR review is meant to detect where state litigation cannot.
relevance.PMC-02: Sovereign immunity forecloses the damages path, leaving audit and oversight mechanisms as the accountability route.
relevance.PMC-04: The court's refusal to reach the merits shows why external fatality and serious-injury review bodies matter in Nebraska.
relevance.PMC-05: The evidentiary record about unreported and unaddressed abuse illustrates the transparency gap public disclosure is meant to close.

cases.case_name: Jill B. & Travis B. v. State
cases.holding: The court held that foster and adoptive parents' claims that the State failed to disclose the placed child's sexual history are barred by the State Tort Claims Act's misrepresentation exception, including any theory framed as an independent operational duty to disclose or warn.
cases.quote: Any operational duty to disclose information or to warn the parents about K.D.M.'s sexual history is subsumed by the misrepresentation exception.

relevance.ACT-03: It defines the legal consequence in Nebraska of an agency's failure to tell a foster home about a placed child's known risk history.
relevance.ACT-04: Kin and non-kin caregivers alike have no damages remedy for non-disclosure at placement.
relevance.OUT-06: Where a placement produces serious harm, the non-disclosure theory is closed off by the misrepresentation exemption.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the companion limitation to Joshua M. on agency liability for harm to children and caregivers in the foster system.
relevance.FAIL-06: Nebraska treats a claimed duty to disclose placement information as sounding in misrepresentation and therefore outside the State's waiver of immunity.
relevance.PMC-05: Because non-disclosure is not actionable, disclosure must be secured through statutory and policy channels rather than tort suits.

cases.case_name: Douglas County v. Anaya
cases.holding: The court held that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 71-519's mandatory newborn metabolic screening is a neutral law of general applicability subject to rational basis review, rejected the parents' free exercise and parental rights challenges, and affirmed the order compelling the testing.
cases.quote: We conclude that the effect of § 71-519 upon the constitutional claims the Anayas have asserted is properly analyzed under a rational basis review.

relevance.INP-07: The case begins with DHHS detecting from health records that a required newborn screening had not been performed, the health-system pathway into State intervention.
relevance.ACT-06: It is Nebraska's controlling authority on court-compelled medical procedures for a child over the parents' religious objection.
relevance.FAIL-05: The court holds that a neutral, generally applicable child health law does not become suspect merely because it burdens a religious practice.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Paxton H.
cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court did not err in ordering DHHS to arrange and pay for the child's placement and services at an out-of-state psychiatric residential treatment facility, and that such a cost order is a final, appealable order.
cases.quote: we conclude that the juvenile court did not err in ordering DHHS to arrange and pay for Paxton to receive services at KidsTLC.

relevance.INP-04: The juvenile court directed the agency's course of action, illustrating judicially driven intervention within an open case.
relevance.ACT-03: It confirms the juvenile court's authority over the agency's placement decisions, including out-of-state residential placements.
relevance.ACT-05: The court's order operates as the protective mechanism where the child cannot safely remain at home and the parents cannot provide needed care.
relevance.ACT-06: It is the Nebraska authority on court-ordered psychiatric residential treatment and who must pay for it.

cases.case_name: Robert M. on behalf of Bella O. v. Danielle O.
cases.holding: The court held that a child is a victim of abuse under the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act where a credible threat, which may be implied from a pattern of conduct, is directed at the child's caretakers and causes them reasonably to fear for the child's safety, and affirmed the protection order entered on the child's behalf.
cases.quote: we conclude that the trial court did not err in determining that Bella was a victim of abuse within the meaning of § 42-903.

relevance.ACT-05: This is the Nebraska Supreme Court's controlling construction of who may obtain a domestic abuse protection order on a child's behalf and what threat evidence suffices.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Rylee S.
cases.holding: The court held that a dispositional order compelling the mother to release her mental health records and submit to a pretreatment assessment was unreasonable because the juvenile court made no supporting findings of fact and the order did not tend to correct or ameliorate the conditions on which the adjudication was based.
cases.quote: we find that the dispositional plan and subsequent order in this case were unreasonable

relevance.ACT-01: Even where services are pursued short of removal, what the court can compel is bounded by the adjudicated conditions.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading Nebraska statement that a court-ordered rehabilitation plan must rest on findings and be reasonably related to reuniting parent and child.
relevance.OUT-01: A plan untethered to the adjudicated conditions cannot advance reunification and will not be sustained on appeal.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process under the Fourteenth Amendment requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence; a fair preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: It fixes the constitutional floor for the proof that must ultimately support State action severing the parent-child relationship, against which agency findings are measured.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional source of the clear-and-convincing standard Nebraska applies in every termination case.
relevance.PMC-06: It is one of the fixed constitutional benchmarks against which a state's termination practice can be systematically scored.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that there is no absolute federal due process right to appointed counsel in parental rights termination proceedings; the Eldridge factors are weighed case by case against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake, and on these facts no counsel was required.
cases.quote: the presumption that there is a right to appointed counsel only where the indigent, if he is unsuccessful, may lose his personal freedom

relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal baseline on counsel in termination cases, which Nebraska exceeds by statute under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-279.01.
relevance.FAIL-01: Denial of counsel is assessed federally under this case-by-case balancing rather than as automatic structural error.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a State to protect a child from violence by a private actor, even where the agency knew of the danger and had intervened, absent a custodial restraint on the child's liberty.
cases.quote: its language cannot fairly be extended to impose an affirmative obligation on the State to ensure that those interests do not come to harm through other means

relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling federal authority foreclosing substantive due process damages claims when a child known to the agency is seriously injured or killed at home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Agency knowledge of danger, without state custody, does not create the special relationship needed for § 1983 liability.
relevance.PMC-04: Because the constitutional remedy is unavailable, fatality and near-fatality review commissions carry the accountability function.
relevance.PMC-06: It marks the outer constitutional limit on holding a child welfare system legally responsible for failure to protect.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that States make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families creates no privately enforceable right under § 1983 or directly under the Act.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans cannot be enforced by a private federal action premised on the IV-E reasonable-efforts clause.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling authority that federal child welfare performance requirements are enforced administratively through funding conditions, not by private suit.
relevance.INP-09: Because private enforcement is unavailable, federal oversight reviews and audits are the operative compliance mechanism.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR review and the withholding of federal funds, not litigation, are the sanctions for a State's failure to meet IV-E requirements.
relevance.PMC-02: Fiscal oversight of the federal conditions is administrative, which is why audit findings carry the enforcement weight.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels exist in part to supply the scrutiny this decision removes from the courts.
relevance.PMC-06: It defines the legal channel through which federal child welfare standards actually bind a state agency.

cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that the father's and children's substantive and procedural due process claims failed because the officials' reliance on the abuse allegations did not shock the conscience and a petition, emergency hearing and post-deprivation hearing followed the removal within days.
cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

relevance.INP-03: The removal arose from a joint law-enforcement and county social services response to a corporal punishment report.
relevance.DEC-02: The court assesses the adequacy of the investigation that preceded removal under the shocks-the-conscience standard.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the current Eighth Circuit statement of the promptness requirement that attaches to any emergency removal, and Nebraska sits in the Eighth Circuit.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody must be followed promptly by a judicial hearing to survive procedural due process review.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the federal § 1983 framework — Fourth Amendment seizure plus procedural and substantive due process — under which a wrongful removal claim from Nebraska would be litigated.

cases.case_name: Riehm v. Engelking
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the student's Fourth Amendment claim but that the social worker's good faith reliance on the ex parte protective custody order was reasonable, so he was entitled to qualified immunity on the seizure claim.
cases.quote: The ex parte order was not so lacking in indicia of probable cause as to render Diercks's reliance on it unreasonable.

relevance.INP-01: The case began when school officials, acting on their reporting obligations, referred a student's disturbing writings to county social services.
relevance.INP-02: It shows how a non-parental report of danger to a child is converted into an emergency protective custody petition.
relevance.INP-08: School staff observations were the sole trigger for the referral and the ensuing removal.
relevance.INP-12: It sets the Eighth Circuit standard for evaluating a protective seizure carried out under an ex parte order.
relevance.DEC-02: The court holds that social workers are expected to take reasonable action on credible indications of danger to a child.
relevance.DEC-04: The validity of the affidavit supporting the ex parte order is the pivot on which the lawfulness of the emergency removal turns.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal is unlawful under this framework where the ex parte order rests on omissions or stale information so serious that reliance on it was unreasonable.

cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed declaratory and permanent injunctive relief against a juvenile officer who removed all of a school's boarding students using stale and inaccurate ex parte petitions and, as to many children, no court order at all, rejecting his claims of judicial and Eleventh Amendment immunity.
cases.quote: Waddle removed all boarding students from HCA without notice or opportunity to be heard, using stale or inaccurate information, and without exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-12: It is the Eighth Circuit's leading case on mass protective custody taken without individualized justification.
relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal requires a court order, probable cause or genuine exigency as to each child, not a blanket sweep.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the controlling circuit authority for Nebraska on § 1983 relief against a child welfare official for unlawful removal, including the unavailability of judicial immunity.

cases.case_name: Shearer v. Leuenberger
cases.holding: The court held that the child abuse immunity provision of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-716 gives the Department's director and investigator state-law immunity for placing a mother's name on the Abused or Neglected Child Registry but does not reach a claim advanced under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and affirmed dismissal because the Department and its officials in their official capacities are not 'persons' under § 1983 and the registry procedures used violated no clearly established right.
cases.quote: the immunity from liability under state law provided by § 28-716 does not apply to a claim advanced under federal law

relevance.INP-02: The § 28-716 immunity the court construes runs to 'any person participating in an investigation or the making of a report,' which is the same provision that shields a non-mandated third-party reporter, and the court fixes its outer limit at maliciously false statements.
relevance.DEC-01: The court sets out the four statutory case-status classifications under § 28-720 — court substantiated, petition to be filed, investigation inconclusive, and unfounded report — and the command that identifying information in unfounded reports be expunged forthwith.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the Nebraska decision the earlier pass identified as the first authority on a maltreatment finding recorded against a parent on the Central Registry, describing the notice given, the preponderance finding required, and the § 28-723 amendment-and-expungement hearing that follows.

cases.case_name: Benitez v. Rasmussen
cases.holding: The court held that in a hearing under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-723 to expunge, amend, or remove a Central Registry report the Department must prove the report's accuracy and consistency by a preponderance of the evidence, that the child-care provider had no protected property interest in her license and no cognizable procedural due process or equal protection claim, and affirmed the refusal to expunge her court-substantiated report.
cases.quote: the Department must prove the accuracy and consistency of a Registry report of child abuse or neglect by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-10: The court sets out the statutory sequence the agency must follow — report received, investigation conducted, and only then a case status determination — which is the escalation from screening to a formal investigative finding.
relevance.DEC-01: It distinguishes the 'unfounded report' and 'investigation inconclusive' classifications from court-substantiated reports and explains that the Department applies different good-cause criteria to expungement of each.
relevance.DEC-03: This is Nebraska's controlling decision on the burden of proof the agency carries to defend a substantiated Central Registry finding and on what process is due the person named in it.
relevance.FAIL-05: The court rejected the equal protection challenge to the Department's use of different expungement criteria for court-substantiated and inconclusive reports, marking the limits of a discrimination claim against registry practice.

cases.case_name: O'Connor v. Kaufman
cases.holding: The court held that an order granting partial summary judgment while reserving damages for later trial is not a final, appealable order because a motion for partial summary judgment is a step in the action rather than a special proceeding, and it disapproved In re Interest of R.G. to the extent that decision suggested Grantham had held otherwise.
cases.quote: we find that the district court's order was not a final, appealable order under the second category because the motion for partial summary judgment did not involve a special proceeding

relevance.INP-12: This is the subsequent-history signal for In re Interest of R.G., the brief's foundational protective-custody due process authority: R.G. stands except on the special-proceeding point disapproved here.
relevance.DEC-04: Any brief relying on R.G. for the affidavit requirement and the post-removal hearing right must carry this disapproval-on-other-grounds citation, which leaves those holdings untouched.
relevance.FAIL-02: It confines the disapproval of R.G. to the final-order analysis, so R.G.'s due process holding remains available to a parent litigating an unlawful removal.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Enyce J. & Eternity M.
cases.holding: The court held that foster parents have no legal or equitable right, title, or interest in the subject matter of a juvenile case, so they lack standing to appeal an order changing the child's placement and are not entitled to intervene as of right, and it disapproved In re Interest of Jorius G. & Cheralee G. and In re Interest of Montana S. to the extent they were inconsistent.
cases.quote: Mark and Roberta did not have a right, title, or interest in the subject matter of the controversy that gave them standing

relevance.ACT-03: This is the foundational Nebraska holding, applied without restatement in In re Interest of Jackson E. and In re Interest of Jordon B., that the statutory role § 43-1314 gives foster parents in the proceeding confers no interest supporting an appeal of a placement decision.
relevance.ACT-04: The juvenile court moved the child to a maternal aunt over the foster parents' objection, and the court held they could neither appeal nor intervene to contest that kinship placement.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Micah H.
cases.holding: The court held that the Nebraska Indian Child Welfare Act's active-efforts provisions in § 43-1503(1) are not a checklist requiring compliance with every subsection but a case-by-case standard, affirmed the findings of active efforts and of willful abandonment proved by clear and convincing evidence, but vacated the adoption decree because the county court did not strictly comply with the consent and criminal-history requirements of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-107.
cases.quote: The conduct constituting abandonment as defined above must appear by clear and convincing evidence to be willful, intentional, or voluntary, without just cause or excuse.

relevance.INP-11: It holds that NICWA's active-efforts requirement governs proceedings terminating rights over an Indian child even where the parent is not of Native American descent, and that § 43-1503(1) is not a compliance checklist — the proposition In re Guardianship of Eliza W. relies on.
relevance.ACT-02: It defines the content of the active-efforts service obligation as a case-by-case, culturally relevant inquiry judged by the individual circumstances rather than a fixed list of services.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the source of the willful-abandonment standard that In re Adoption of Kate S. applies when petitioners seek to dispense with a parent's consent to adoption.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of R.R.
cases.holding: The court held that a short-term ex parte temporary detention order is not final while an order entered after a detention hearing that continues to keep custody from the parent pending adjudication is appealable, and that on this record due process did not require the mother's counsel to be present at the temporary detention hearing because the juvenile court refused to take notice of that testimony at adjudication and she was represented at every later stage.
cases.quote: considering the procedures used in this case, due process did not require the presence of the mother's counsel at the temporary detention hearing

relevance.INP-12: It is the companion decided months after In re Interest of R.G. and cited alongside it in In re Interest of Borius H., fixing when an order taking or continuing protective custody becomes reviewable and what process the parent is owed at the detention hearing.
relevance.DEC-04: It draws the line between the unappealable short-term ex parte detention order and the appealable order that continues removal after hearing, which is the procedural frame around every emergency removal decision.
relevance.DEC-05: The court refused to review the sufficiency of the juvenile petition because the petition was never made part of the record, an evidentiary discipline that governs any challenge to the petition opening a dependency case.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Nicole M.
cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of the mother's parental rights but held that the State failed to rebut the presumption that the father was a fit parent and reversed the termination of his rights, declining to reach the hearsay and best-interests questions.
cases.quote: before a court may terminate parental rights, the State must also show that the parent is unfit

relevance.INP-12: This is the decision In re Interest of Carmelo G. cites for its premise that the proper starting point for legal analysis when the State involves itself in family relations is always the fundamental constitutional rights of a parent.
relevance.DEC-04: That fundamental-rights premise is what makes an emergency removal a constitutionally constrained decision rather than an ordinary administrative one, and it is the footing for Nebraska's post-removal due process cases.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed the termination of the father's rights because the State never rebutted the presumption of his fitness, correcting an agency case built on a failure-to-protect theory.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Brian B. et al.
cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court properly exercised its discretion in allowing the child to testify in chambers with counsel present, that the procedures used adequately safeguarded the father's due process rights, and that the allegations of the petition were proved by a preponderance of the evidence, affirming the adjudication of all three children under § 43-247(3)(a).
cases.quote: The purpose of the adjudication phase of a juvenile proceeding is to protect the interests of the child.

relevance.DEC-03: It shows what evidence of sexual abuse will sustain a finding by a preponderance at adjudication, and approves in-chambers child testimony as an acceptable means of receiving it.
relevance.DEC-05: It is the authority In re Interest of Xandria P. relies on for the framework the brief uses at this node: the adjudication phase exists to protect the child, and the parents' rights are determined at disposition, not at adjudication.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Becka P. et al.
cases.holding: The court held that the orders appointing an educational surrogate were final, appealable orders because they were unlimited in duration and scope and affected the parents' substantial right to direct their child's education, that the juvenile court retained power to issue and rule upon orders to show cause while the adjudications were on appeal, and affirmed.
cases.quote: we conclude these were not temporary orders, but, rather, orders which affected the parents' substantial right to direct the education of their child

relevance.ACT-02: The juvenile court's appointment of an educational surrogate after the parents refused to sign assessment authorizations shows how far a court-ordered service and evaluation plan can reach into parental decision-making.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the appellate-jurisdiction authority In re Interest of Paxton H. cites for the duty to confirm jurisdiction in a juvenile appeal before any agency or juvenile court decision can be reviewed at all.
relevance.OUT-05: Whether a juvenile court order is final determines whether an appeal is decided on the merits or dismissed without one.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of J.M.N.
cases.holding: The court held that an order directing the Department of Social Services to pay the costs of a ward's treatment is a final, appealable order, but that the Department is not a 'parent' within Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-290, so the order requiring it to pay for the juvenile's alcohol treatment was void from its inception and was reversed.
cases.quote: An order which directs DSS to pay for the costs of treatment is a final order for purposes of § 25-1902.

relevance.INP-04: A juvenile court order directing the agency to obtain and pay for a ward's treatment is the court-driven form of intervention, and the court holds such an order is void unless the statute actually reaches the agency.
relevance.ACT-03: It supplies the finality rule — an order directing the agency to pay a ward's treatment costs is appealable — that is the jurisdictional predicate In re Interest of Paxton H. rests on.
relevance.ACT-06: It is the earliest Nebraska authority on who bears the cost when a court orders medical or psychological treatment for a child already in state custody.

cases.case_name: In re Interest of Jahon S.
cases.holding: The court held that the § 43-292(2) statutory ground was established by the father's neglect of the child's siblings and that termination of the incarcerated father's parental rights was in the child's best interests, affirming the termination.
cases.quote: Although incarceration alone cannot be the sole basis for terminating parental rights, it is a factor to be considered.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the published Nebraska Supreme Court holding, in the majority opinion, that incarceration alone cannot be the sole basis for terminating parental rights but is a factor, together with the rule that the criminal conduct causing the incarceration is voluntary.

cases.case_name: Maria A. on behalf of Leslie G. v. Oscar G.
cases.holding: The court held that whether abuse within the meaning of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 42-903 occurred is the threshold question at a § 42-925 show-cause hearing, that a court may then also weigh factors bearing on the likelihood of future harm in deciding whether the order should remain in effect, and affirmed rescission of the ex parte protection order a mother had obtained on her child's behalf.
cases.quote: Whether domestic abuse occurred is a threshold issue in determining whether an ex parte protection order should be affirmed

relevance.ACT-05: It is the companion to Robert M. on behalf of Bella O. on the protective-order route for a child: the petitioner must first establish statutory abuse, and even then the court decides prospectively whether the order should remain in effect.

cases.case_name: OMNI Behavioral Health v. Nebraska Foster Care Review Bd.
cases.holding: The court held that the State Foster Care Review Board's statutory authority under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-1303 to visit and observe foster care facilities is not facially unconstitutional for want of implementing regulations, and that any Fourth Amendment or state constitutional challenge to a particular home visit must be judged case by case under a reasonableness standard, affirming summary judgment for the Board.
cases.quote: any claim that a home visit by the State Board infringes upon Fourth Amendment rights, or corresponding rights under the Nebraska Constitution, must be judged by a standard of reasonableness

relevance.INP-09: The Board's statewide foster care register, its case reviews, and its reports to DHHS, county welfare offices and the courts are the Nebraska oversight machinery through which systemic problems surface and prompt further agency or court action.
relevance.PMC-03: This is the Nebraska Supreme Court's description of the State Foster Care Review Board and its local boards — Nebraska's independent placement review bodies and the closest state analogue to a CAPTA § 5106a(c) citizen review panel — and of the visits and reporting through which they exercise that review.

NO unpublished memorandum decisions were used.

Calkins (former ward program eligibility) is the closest Nebraska authority and is mapped there; practitioners should treat OUT-04 as governed primarily by statute and by the federal Chafee/FCSIAA framework.

In re Interest of B.B. notes that the only Nebraska case citing the reporter-immunity statute Sec. 28-716 in a registry context is Shearer v. Leuenberger, 256 Neb. 566, 591 N.W.2d 762 (1999) (state actors individually immune after a mother's name was entered on the Abused or Neglected Child Registry), disapproved on other grounds by Simon v. Shearer was NOT independently retrieved and read in this session and is therefore deliberately excluded from cases[]; it is flagged here as the first authority a lawyer should pull for that node.

The two cases mapped (In re Interest of DeWayne G., Jr. for the Sec. 43-283.01 duty to make efforts before foster placement; In re Interest of Carmelo G. for safety plans used to avert removal) are the nearest state-law analogues, and this node is at the 2-case floor as a result.

GAP — discrimination / retaliation (FAIL-05): no published Nebraska appellate decision was found applying the ADA, Section 504, or the Multiethnic Placement Act to a child welfare case. The only responsive hit was In re Interest of Audrey B. (Neb. Ct. App. July 3, 2023), which is an unpublished memorandum web opinion carrying the notice that it 'IS NOT DESIGNATED FOR PERMANENT PUBLICATION AND MAY NOT BE CITED EXCEPT AS PROVIDED BY NEB. CT. R. APP. P. Sec. 2-102(E)'; it is therefore excluded. FAIL-05 is populated with the ICWA line of cases (Walter W., Eliza W., Mercedes L.) and Douglas County v. GAP — PMC oversight nodes (PMC-01 through PMC-06) and INP-09: there is no Nebraska case law on CFSR reviews, Citizen Review Panels under CAPTA Sec. 5106a(c), the Protect Our Kids Act commission, or federal OIG audits. Those nodes are populated with the governing federal standard — Suter v. Artist M. (federal child welfare requirements are enforced through funding conditions and administrative review, not private suit) and DeShaney (no constitutional duty to protect) — plus the Nebraska public-records and sovereign-immunity decisions that determine what a citizen can actually obtain or recover in this state. This is the federal-standard fallback the instructions contemplate, not on-point state authority.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the NE node files are keyword-matched noise: they are dominated by recent probate, estate, trust, and adult guardianship listings (In re Estate of Walker, In re Masek Family Trust, In re Guardianship & Conservatorship of Dietz, etc.) carrying synthetic Justia docket-style identifiers rather than reporter citations. None survived retrieval and review; none are retained. Titles that were checked and are genuine but off-point for these nodes include the adult guardianship/conservatorship line. In re Adoption of Kate S. and In re Adoption of Faith F. appeared in that noise and Kate S. was independently retrieved, read and retained.

Duplicate CourtListener clusters exist for several Nebraska opinions (e.g. In re Interest of Denzel D. at clusters 9413443 and 9411987; In re Interest of Joseph C. at 4521256 and 8283574; In re Interest of Paxton H. at 4539203 and 8284530). The cluster_id given is the one whose opinion text was actually retrieved and read; for Paxton H. that is cluster 8284530, styled by CourtListener as 'Neb. Dep't of Health & Human Servs. v. Penny H. (In re Interest of Paxton H.)' but reported as In re Interest of Paxton H., 300 Neb. 446.

Citation form note: CourtListener stores Nebraska Court of Appeals citations as 'Neb. Ct. App.'; they are rendered here in Bluebook form as 'Neb. App.' (e.g. 29 Neb. App. 1; 26 Neb. App. 737). In re Interest of Denzel D., In re Interest of Jessalina M., In re Adoption of Kate S., Joshua M. v. State and Jill B. & Travis B. v. State had no N.W.2d citation in the cluster record, so only the Nebraska Reports cite is given.

Practice point for families and counsel: the two most load-bearing Nebraska rules in this chain are (1) an ex parte temporary custody order must be supported by an affidavit of someone with personal knowledge, and at the detention hearing the State must prove the Sec. 43-254 grounds by a preponderance (In re Interest of R.G.; In re Interest of Borius H.), and (2) the post-removal hearing must follow without unreasonable delay, with an eight-month gap held unconstitutional (In re Interest of Carmelo G.). Conversely, a parent has no right to demand a separate reasonable-efforts hearing before termination (In re Interest of DeWayne G., Jr.), and foster parents and kin caregivers have no right to intervene or to appeal placement decisions (In re Interest of Jackson E.; In re Interest of Jordon B.).

Practice point on remedies: Nebraska's sovereign immunity decisions close most damages routes against DHHS for harm to children in care — Joshua M. v. State (assault-or-battery exemption bars negligence claims arising from a foster parent's abuse) and Jill B. & Travis B. v. State (misrepresentation exemption bars failure-to-disclose claims). Federal Sec. 1983 relief against individual officials for unlawful removal remains available in the Eighth Circuit under Heartland Academy v. Waddle, Riehm v. Engelking and Mitchell v. Dakota County, but DeShaney forecloses failure-to-protect claims where the child was never in state custody.

API budget: 135 of the allotted 150 CourtListener requests were used, paced at one request per 2.1 seconds, with all responses cached locally so that re-reading opinions cost no additional requests. One request returned a read timeout (the Heartland cluster metadata) and was retried once successfully; no other errors occurred and no request was looped on failure.
